p: In this message Pastor David G. Kincer continues the series by listing the requirements of a judge from Exodus 18, Deuteronomy 1 and 2 Chronicles 19, and shows how God judged Judah when the people failed to correct their leaders. He then teaches how the righteous and the wicked grow together, using Proverbs, and calls Christians to stand for Bible morality, persuading, warning and teaching.
What requirements does the Bible give for a judge? (Exodus 18:21)

He says Exodus 18:21 and other passages give ten requirements of a judge, starting with “fear God,” which he defines as “depart from evil and hate evil.” He adds that judges must be men of truth, “not feelings, not emotions, not opinion,” and must hate covetousness.
What requirements does the Bible give for a judge? (Exodus 18:21)

Now 10 requirements of a judge. This is interesting. And this is where our constitution failed us. There’s no requirement of character to be a politician in our constitution. That’s where the constitution came up short. Number one, Exodus 18:21, fear God. Now, how many remember what fear God is? Depart from evil and hate evil. Say it. Hate evil. Depart from evil. The Bible says that’s the fear of God. Always use your Bible definitions. See, when I fear God, I will depart from evil. I not only will depart from it, but like Noah who hated evil and Job hated evil. They despised it. How many could use a little dose of hatred for sin? Yeah. So you don’t do it. Yeah. Now number two, they got to be men of truth. People of truth. See, not feelings, not emotions, not opinion, but truth. And they got to hate covetousness, the desire for something that’s not yours. To where you get it. You see, you desire somebody else’s spouse and you do whatever is necessary to get it. That’s covetousness. You desire your neighbor’s car. You don’t work, get an education to buy one, so you go steal it. That’s covetousness.
What requirements does the Bible give for a judge? (Exodus 18:21)

Exodus 18:21: Moreover you shall select from all the people able men, such as fear God, men of truth, hating covetousness; and place such over them to be rulers of thousands, rulers of hundreds, rulers of fifties, and rulers of tens.
Must a judge treat everyone the same? (Deuteronomy 1:16-17)

He says a judge must “judge rightly” and treat everybody the same, “the small, the great, your brother, your family member, your church member, the stranger, the foreigner.” He says that means anyone who breaks the law is dealt with by it, and that laws should be made so people can come in legally with dignity and work.
Must a judge treat everyone the same? (Deuteronomy 1:16-17)

And judges cannot covet. In Deuteronomy 1:16. Number four, you got to judge rightly. All right? And you got to treat everybody the same. The small, the great, your brother, your family member, your church member, the stranger, the foreigner, they all got to abide by the same law. And that means if I live in Mexico and I come to America illegally, I have to be dealt with by the law. Just like if an American did something illegally, but not our Congress. Now, I know the Mexicans don’t appreciate this, but let me tell you, it’s the truth. And you go to Mexico illegally and see what happens. We just got a bunch of pansy congress people. That’s all. You know what they should do is make laws where these people can come in legally with dignity and work. Hallelujah. That’s just an example. No respecter of persons in judgment. And let me tell you something. When our chaplain in the military cannot stand up for the Bible because of the homosexuals, that’s respecter of persons.
Must a judge treat everyone the same? (Deuteronomy 1:16-17)

Deuteronomy 1:16-17: “Then I commanded your judges at that time, saying, ‘Hear the cases between your brethren, and judge righteously between a man and his brother or the stranger who is with him. You shall not show partiality in judgment; you shall hear the small as well as the great; you shall not be afraid in any man’s presence, for the judgment is God’s. The case that is too hard for you, bring to me, and I will hear it.’
Does he call it a culture war or a Bible war?
He says “it’s not a culture war,” it’s “a Bible war,” “a Jesus war,” because “they don’t like Jesus and they don’t like the Bible.” He says “we let them tame us with their thinking.”
Does he call it a culture war or a Bible war?

And that’s not a cultural war. Bill O’Reilly’s got that one wrong, too. It is a Bible and Jesus war. They’re trying to get rid of the Bible and they’re trying to get rid of Jesus. And O’Reilly uses it culture. I hate that. It’s not a culture war. They’re totally against the Bible and Jesus Christ who is for right Bible morality. Can I hear an amen? And see, we let them tame us with their thinking. A culture war. Cultural war. What’s a cultural war? It’s a Bible war. It’s a Jesus war. They don’t like Jesus and they don’t like the Bible. You will not be afraid of the face of men, these small and great, for the judgment is the Lord’s.
Does he call it a culture war or a Bible war?

Deuteronomy 1:17: You shall not show partiality in judgment; you shall hear the small as well as the great; you shall not be afraid in any man’s presence, for the judgment is God’s. The case that is too hard for you, bring to me, and I will hear it.’
Why must a judge not be afraid of the rich and powerful?

He says a judge “can’t be afraid of their stature,” their position or their money, and “has to be strong and do what’s right no matter what the threat or repercussions are.” He applies it to parents who water down discipline because they fear their child will not like them.
Why must a judge not be afraid of the rich and powerful?

And this is why a lot of people won’t judge. Like you get a rich man or a politician, they get away with things, don’t they? And a judge can’t be afraid of their stature. They can’t be afraid of their position. They can’t be afraid of their money. They can’t be afraid because they’re [unclear] and going to kill their family and everything else if we judge them. A judge has to be strong and do what’s right no matter what the threat or repercussions are. Wow. Well, if I correct my child, he won’t like me anymore. Well, it’s tough, isn’t it? So, I let my child be a bird brain because I don’t want him not liking me.
What did Jehoshaphat tell the judges he appointed? (2 Chronicles 19:5-7)

He says Jehoshaphat told the judges to “take heed,” be alert, know the laws, fear the Lord, and remember that “there’s no injustice with God.” He says there is no respect of persons and no taking bribes, and that “there’s one Bible,” not a Catholic, Protestant or Jewish one.
What did Jehoshaphat tell the judges he appointed? (2 Chronicles 19:5-7)

See, it’s in the family. Hallelujah. Well, if I really discipline him, he’ll run away. That’s his choice. I’m going to water down what he needs to learn because I’m afraid of him running away. Hallelujah. Are you there folks? You judge. See, parents have got to learn this stuff. We go to Jehoshaphat in 2 Chronicles 19:5. Jehoshaphat judges over the people and he gave him qualifications. Take heed. Be alert. Be attentive and get your homework done. Know the laws. Be cautious. All right. And then he repeats the fear of the Lord. He said, ‘There’s no injustice with God. God is never unfair. What’s good for men is good for women. What’s good for whites is good for blacks. What’s good for poor is good for rich. Judgment is never unfair. Hallelujah. See, Catholic or Protestant, you’re not excused because you’re a Catholic and they believe certain things that you can’t use that excuse. He says it is anything given to influence a decision, giving examples from courts and business, and says you should get a product “because it’s the best on the market for the best price, not because someone is giving you something.”
How does he say we should treat people who oppose Bible morality?
He says “we are to contend with them and fight with them, but at the same time, we are to what? Persuade them, warn them, and teach them to avoid that judgment of God. That’s the balance of it.”
How many does he say died in the plague after David’s census?
He says “70,000 people died by the plague,” and that God was not unjust, because “they violated the law” and the people did not correct David.
How long does he say God waited before judging Judah?
He says “He waited 400 years to do this,” sending prophets “and everything else” but the people would not listen.
What does he mean by people in “white” and “red” on his slides?

He says the people in white are those for Christ and Bible morality, and the people in red are those who “want to sin,” “want to disobey God,” and want to violate Bible morals. The slides are not shown in the transcript.
What does he say happens when the wicked perish?
He says “when who perishes? The wicked. The righteous increase,” and that if the foundations are removed, “the righteous has to find a way to get rid of the wicked.”
What does he say is wrong with the church in America?
He says the church “has been dumbed down by faith and grace and a lot of other stuff distracting us from Bible morality to where we allow people to live in open sin without even challenging them.”
What does he say about legislating Bible morality?
He says “they say you can’t legislate Bible morality, but it’s okay for the atheists and the homosexuals to legislate their morality,” and asks, “are we that dumb?”

items.d: In this short message Pastor David G. Kincer teaches that God judges and punishes His people when they behave worse than Sodom. He uses Jude 1:7 and Luke 17:28 to show Sodom as an example and argues that the…
p: In this short message Pastor David G. Kincer teaches that God judges and punishes His people when they behave worse than Sodom. He uses Jude 1:7 and Luke 17:28 to show Sodom as an example and argues that the Bible, not science, tells us what is an allegory. He then begins Ezekiel 16, where God lists abominations His people commit, starting with trusting in your own beauty and playing the harlot because of your fame.
Does God judge and punish His own people?
He says “God judges, and He punishes His people when His people behave worse than Sodom did.” He asks “what can be worse than that city of Sodom?” and says they will find out in this message.
Does God judge and punish His own people?

But today we’re going to look at the fact is, God judges, and He punishes His people when His people behave worse than Sodom did. Did you say, God’s people behave worse than Sodom? Sodom and Gomorrah, yes, we’re going to find out today. And what is worse than Sodom? What can be worse than that city of Sodom?
Why is Sodom a biblical example of God’s vengeance? (Jude 1:7)

He says Sodom is “a biblical illustration of God punishing people.” He cites Jude 1:7, that Sodom and Gomorrah gave themselves over to “sexual immorality and strange flesh,” and says sexual immorality includes adultery and sex before marriage.
Why is Sodom a biblical example of God’s vengeance? (Jude 1:7)

Sodom, we’re going to make a statement that Sodom is a biblical illustration of God’s vengeance. Okay, it’s a biblical illustration of God punishing people. In Jude’s chapter 1:7, the only chapter in Jude: “Sodom and Gomorrah, and the cities round about them, having given themselves over to sexual immorality and strange flesh.” Homosexuality. Two things he mentions is what? Sexual immorality. That’s adultery, sex before marriage, sex in marriage with somebody outside your marriage, marriage.
Why is Sodom a biblical example of God’s vengeance? (Jude 1:7)

Jude 1:7: as Sodom and Gomorrah, and the cities around them in a similar manner to these, having given themselves over to sexual immorality and gone after strange flesh, are set forth as an example, suffering the vengeance of eternal fire.
What does it mean that Sodom is “an example, an illustration”?

He says incest, orgies, bestiality and homosexuality are included and are “set forth as an example, an illustration, suffering the vengeance of God.” Because the Bible calls it an example, he says, “we want to use illustrations, we want to use the right one.”
What does it mean that Sodom is “an example, an illustration”?

Uh, uh, incest, orgies, bestiality, all these things are included, and homosexuality, are set forth as an example, an illustration, “suffering the vengeance of God.” You see, the Bible said it was an example, it was an illustration, and we want to use illustrations, we want to use the right one.
Who decides what is an allegory or an example in the Bible?

He says “we cannot use examples unless the Bible uses them. The Bible is the one that’s got to tell us what the examples, the allegories, and the metaphors are.” Those who say the Bible is a book of allegories and myths “by using science for their reason” are wrong, he says.
Who decides what is an allegory or an example in the Bible?

We cannot use examples unless the Bible uses them. The Bible is the one that’s got to tell us what the examples, the allegories, and the metaphors are. So Bill O’Reilly, homosexual atheists, humanists, and liberal activists are wrong when they say the Bible is a book of allegories and myths, by using science for their reason. They say--
Does science prove the Bible’s accounts are only allegory?

He says science is used to claim that the ark, the flood and Jonah’s fish are allegories, but “science can’t prove that they could happen.” He says “God is supernatural, and He can do anything He chooses when He chooses.”
Does science prove the Bible’s accounts are only allegory?

See, science says you can’t get all the animals on the ark, so it’s an allegory. Science says the earth wasn’t flooded, so it’s an allegory. Science says that there’s no fish that could swallow a human being and the human being live, because of the stomach acids and so forth and the lack of oxygen. Because science says you can’t go to the Bible and say these things are allegories and examples, they never happened, because science can’t prove that they could happen. God is supernatural, and He can do anything He chooses when He chooses.
When does the Bible itself use a parable, symbol or illustration?

He says the Bible becomes an allegory, parable or symbol when Jesus says so, such as “I’m telling you a parable.” Jesus then used natural truth, like sowers sowing seed and mustard trees growing from seed, to give spiritual illustrations.
When does the Bible itself use a parable, symbol or illustration?

The only time the Bible becomes an allegory, a parable, a symbol: Jesus said, “I’m telling you a parable.” He says, “I’m giving you a symbol, I’m giving you an illustration,” and then He used the natural truth to give us spiritual what? Illustrations. See, sowers did sow seed, mustard trees did grow from seed. Are you there?
What does Jesus say about the days of Lot and His return? (Luke 17:28)

He says we can use something as an example only when the Bible states it, as in Jude 1:7 and Luke 17:28, where Jesus speaks of “the days of Lot.” So when Jesus comes a second time, he says, “we have the example of what Sodom and Gomorrah, to go back to and figure out what’s going to happen there.”
What does Jesus say about the days of Lot and His return? (Luke 17:28)

We can only do this when it states that it’s an example and an illustration, as in Jude 1:7 that we just quoted you. Luke 17:28, where Jesus said, “Likewise the coming of the Son of Man shall it be in the days of Lot.” So see, when Jesus comes the second time, we have the example of what Sodom and Gomorrah, to go back to and figure out what’s going to happen there.
What does Jesus say about the days of Lot and His return? (Luke 17:28)

Luke 17:28-30: Likewise as it was also in the days of Lot: They ate, they drank, they bought, they sold, they planted, they built; but on the day that Lot went out of Sodom it rained fire and brimstone from heaven and destroyed them all. Even so will it be in the day when the Son of Man is revealed.
What does Ezekiel 16 say God’s people are judged for?
Reading Ezekiel 16:2, he says “God judges His people for abominations,” and “an abomination is something God hates.” He says God will give six abominations that His people do.
What does Ezekiel 16 say God’s people are judged for?

Ezekiel 16:2. We’re going to find that God judges His people for abominations. His people do abominations, yes. He’s going to give us six abominations that God’s people do. How many? Six. An abomination is something God hates, and see, we think that the homosexual last week was abominable, that’s just an abomination.
What does Ezekiel 16 say God’s people are judged for?
Ezekiel 16:2: “Son of man, cause Jerusalem to know her abominations,
What does “you trusted in your own beauty” mean? (Ezekiel 16:15)

He says the first abomination in Ezekiel 16:15 is “You trusted in your own beauty,” and that God hates it. He says you must understand the biblical definition of beauty, which is “not how good your hair looks” or the latest fashion designer clothes, and he gives 1 Chronicles 16:29, to worship the Lord in the beauty of “right living.”
What does “you trusted in your own beauty” mean? (Ezekiel 16:15)

Well, God’s going to give us six more abominations. And homosexuality is abomination, sexual immorality is abomination. God hates it, He detests it, and He’s given us six that His people do that He hates. Has he got your attention? Number one, Ezekiel 16:15: “You trusted in your own beauty.” It’s abomination. Well, how do I trust in my own beauty? Well, you got to understand the biblical definition of beauty, and it’s not how good your hair looks, and if you got the latest fashion designer clothes on. 1 Chronicles 16:29: “Worship the Lord in the beauty of” what? Oh, right.
What does “you trusted in your own beauty” mean? (Ezekiel 16:15)

Ezekiel 16:15: “But you trusted in your own beauty, played the harlot because of your fame, and poured out your harlotry on everyone passing by who would have it. 1 Chronicles 16:29: Give to the LORD the glory due His name; Bring an offering, and come before Him. Oh, worship the LORD in the beauty of holiness!
What happens when a righteous man trusts in his own righteousness? (Ezekiel 33:13)

He says trusting in your own beauty means trusting “what you determined was right in your own eyes. That’s an abomination. We got to trust in what the Bible says is right.” Citing Ezekiel 33:13, he says that if the righteous man trusts in his own righteousness and commits iniquity, “die for it, just like the Sodomites.”
What happens when a righteous man trusts in his own righteousness? (Ezekiel 33:13)

Living. He said, “You trusted in your own beauty,” what you determined was right in your own eyes. That’s an abomination. We got to trust in what the Bible says is right. Is that a good amen or an old me? Uh, is that a place where you slap yourself and go, “Wake up,” silly? Ezekiel 33:13: “If the righteous man”--he’s talking about the righteous man--“if the righteous man turns from his righteousness and begins to trust in his own righteousness,” his own beauty, all right, “and he commits iniquity,” he will what? Die for it, just like the Sodomites.
What happens when a righteous man trusts in his own righteousness? (Ezekiel 33:13)

Ezekiel 33:13: When I say to the righteous that he shall surely live, but he trusts in his own righteousness and commits iniquity, none of his righteous works shall be remembered; but because of the iniquity that he has committed, he shall die.
What does “you played the harlot because of your fame” mean? (Ezekiel 16:15)

He says Ezekiel is speaking to God’s people: “He’s not talking to sinners, he’s talking to his people.” The second abomination, he says, is “You played the harlot because of your fame,” trusting in being famous and popular throughout the world.
What does “you played the harlot because of your fame” mean? (Ezekiel 16:15)

Did. And he’s talking to his people now. He’s not talking to sinners, he’s talking to his people. Hallelujah. Number two abomination, number two: “You played the harlot because of your fame.” You know, you’re famous throughout the world. You go to Joel Osteen’s church, man, you’re popular. You go to Crystal Cathedral, you’re popular. You’re a Catholic, you got a pope, a new pope over there in, in, uh, the Vatican who believes in civil marriages, unions, same-sex unions. I checked up on this old boy, he’s not this little humble Jesuit priest that they want to exalt. He’s got some beliefs that are anti-Bible.
What does “you played the harlot because of your fame” mean? (Ezekiel 16:15)
Ezekiel 16:15: “But you trusted in your own beauty, played the harlot because of your fame, and poured out your harlotry on everyone passing by who would have it.
What is a harlot in the Bible?

He says a harlot is one who hires herself out, and “a harlot in the Bible is also one that just has intimate relationships with people outside the marriage,” wanting to be satisfied by someone outside their family, home, spouse or marriage.
What is a harlot in the Bible?

A harlot is one that hires herself out, as we heard Friday night here in the [unclear], they sell themselves. A harlot in the Bible is also one that just has intimate relationships with people outside the marriage. Don’t have to hire themselves out, they just want to be satisfied by someone outside their family, their home, their spouse, their marriage. Okay.
What does chasing popularity cost your relationship with Jesus?

He says that when you are so popular that everybody likes you, “you have broken your relationship with Jesus Christ and His Word to let these people satisfy you and indoctrinate you.” He moves on to the third abomination, that you “poured out your harlotry on everyone passing by.”
What does chasing popularity cost your relationship with Jesus?

He says, “And you’ve played the harlot because of your fame.” You are so popular, everybody likes you, everybody thinks that you’re great. You have broken your relationship with Jesus Christ and His Word to let these people satisfy you and indoctrinate you. He goes on to say, number three, not only did you do this, but “you poured out your harlotry on everyone passing by who would have”--
What does chasing popularity cost your relationship with Jesus?
Ezekiel 16:15: “But you trusted in your own beauty, played the harlot because of your fame, and poured out your harlotry on everyone passing by who would have it.
What does he say is worse than Sodom?
He says God’s people can behave worse than Sodom did, and that God “judges, and He punishes His people” when they do.
What does he say sexual immorality includes?
He says it is “adultery, sex before marriage, sex in marriage with somebody outside your marriage,” and that incest, orgies, bestiality and homosexuality are also included.
Does he say the Bible is a book of allegories and myths?
No. He says the Bible must tell us which are the examples, allegories and metaphors, and that those who call it “a book of allegories and myths” are wrong.
Can science disprove the ark, the flood or the fish that swallowed a man?
He says science says these cannot have happened, but “science can’t prove that they could happen. God is supernatural, and He can do anything He chooses when He chooses.”
When does he say the Bible is a parable?
He says the Bible becomes a parable or symbol when it says so, such as Jesus saying “I’m telling you a parable.”
What does he say an abomination is?
He says “an abomination is something God hates.”
What does he say is the biblical definition of beauty?
He says it is “not how good your hair looks” or the latest fashion designer clothes. He points to 1 Chronicles 16:29, worshiping the Lord in the beauty of right living.
What does he say it means to trust in your own beauty or righteousness?
He says it means trusting “what you determined was right in your own eyes,” rather than “what the Bible says is right.”
Is Ezekiel 16 speaking to sinners or to God’s people?
He says “he’s not talking to sinners, he’s talking to his people.”
Does “harlot” only mean someone who sells themselves?

No. He says a harlot is one who hires herself out, but in the Bible it also means someone who has intimate relationships with people outside the marriage and just wants “to be satisfied by someone outside their family, their home, their spouse, their marriage.”

items.d: In this message Pastor David G. Kincer teaches from Isaiah 34 and Revelation 6 about God’s dealing with the Gentiles: the ungodly and secular humanists. He argues that the stars falling and the sun darkening…
p: In this message Pastor David G. Kincer teaches from Isaiah 34 and Revelation 6 about God’s dealing with the Gentiles: the ungodly and secular humanists. He argues that the stars falling and the sun darkening are not allegory, that Esau and the ten virgins show a door that closes, and that God’s purpose in judgment is to win the nations to Christ. He closes with two family stories to show how far parents go for their children, and says God wants even his opponents to live.
Who are the Gentiles in Isaiah 34, and what does God ask of them?

He says Isaiah 34 is “God’s word to the Gentiles,” meaning “the ungodly, the heathen, the nations, the people that don’t believe in Jesus.” He says God asks two things of them, “hear, number one, and heed, number two,” and that the church has the responsibility to speak because “without a preacher” they cannot hear.
Who are the Gentiles in Isaiah 34, and what does God ask of them?

In Isaiah 34, he’s going to directly deal with the Gentiles. This session is entitled “God’s Word to the Gentiles,” the ungodly, the heathen, the nations, the people that don’t believe in Jesus, don’t believe that the Bible is God’s word and truth, they don’t follow Jesus. So Isaiah 34:1, “Come near, you Gentiles,” this is how Isaiah starts out. Now, he’s been hitting the church pretty hard for the last 30 chapters, but now Isaiah has focused his attention on the unchurched, the ungodly. “Come near, you Gentiles, come near,” and that’s what Jesus, “Come unto me, all you that labor and are heavy laden, I will give you rest.” And there’s two things that God asked for the Gentiles to do: hear, number one, and heed, number two. If we don’t obey the word, it doesn’t do us any good to have heard the word. And how are they going to hear? The Bible says, without a preacher, and so the church has the responsibility of speaking up for truth. Could that be an amen? And it isn’t like God’s going to speak from heaven, “You Gentiles,” he’s going to send you to speak to them and to get them to obey the word of God. The people is the Gentiles that he’s talking to. “Let the earth hear, and all that is in it.” Now, the earth is a specific
Who are the Gentiles in Isaiah 34, and what does God ask of them?

Isaiah 34:1-2: Come near, you nations, to hear; And heed, you people! Let the earth hear, and all that is in it, The world and all things that come forth from it. For the indignation of the LORD is against all nations, And His fury against all their armies; He has utterly destroyed them, He has given them over to the slaughter. Matthew 11:28: Come to Me, all you who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.
What does he say about life in space and God’s anger at the nations?

He says “there’s only one Earth,” that “there is no life out there in space,” and that “science fiction is exactly what it is, fiction.” He says God’s “fury is against all their armies,” and that an army can also be the word, used to convince people of a philosophy.
What does he say about life in space and God’s anger at the nations?

planet. It’s not Mars, it’s not Jupiter, it’s not some earthlike planet ultra light years away. There’s only one Earth, there’s only one civilization that God made, there is no life out there in space, the Bible never says there is, he always speaks to the planet Earth. Can I hear an amen? Hallelujah. Science fiction is exactly what it is, fiction, all right, I love it, but it’s fiction. “The world,” or mankind, the world is mankind and all things that come from mankind, “come near and hear.” So he’s directly addressing those that are not his people. Verse 2, “For the indignation,” or anger, “the wrath of the Lord is against all the Gentiles.” Okay, he’s angry. None of you have ever been angry, you wouldn’t understand that, but God’s angry. “His fury is against all their armies.” The army is the authority, the might that a people, uh, use to force their propaganda on others or defend their philosophies from others, and an army that we forget about is the word. A lot of people use the word, and they convince people with the army of the word, speaking information, knowledge, to convince people, and we forget that it’s not always swords and spears and, and, uh, atomic bombs and so
What does he mean by “past tense,” and what is secular humanism?

He says Isaiah speaks of the Gentiles’ destruction in the past tense because “God has ordained it and it’s going to happen,” as Jesus “died before the foundation of the world.” He reads Psalm 9:19 and then says secular humanism is a group of Gentiles in our day, and quotes the humanist manifesto as saying there is no God and that the Bible is a book of myths.
What does he mean by “past tense,” and what is secular humanism?

forth. “He’s utterly destroyed,” past tense, he’s utterly destroyed them, “he has given them over to slaughter,” past tense. You see, it’s just like the Bible says that Jesus died before the foundation of the world, God, and the Bible also says in Revelation that Jesus was the beginning of creation, before anything else, God the Son, Jesus was the plan, he died, all right, past tense, before he said, “Let there be light.” Jesus had died, past tense, and then he came in the flesh and died for the sins of the world and caused it to happen. This is the same terminology here, past tense. God has ordained it and it’s going to happen, whether you like it or not, whether you believe in it or not, it’s as good as done, past tense. Amen. Psalm 9:19, “Let not man prevail, put them in fear, oh Lord, that the Gentiles may know themselves to be but men.” See, this is the cry of the Holy Spirit: Lord, put them in fear, so that mankind comes to the understanding that they’re just humans and you are the supernatural God. Hallelujah. So we just happen to have a group of people in our day that are Gentiles, ungodly, they’re called the religion of secular humanism. This is the global icon of the secular humanist movement all over the world, trying to spread their propaganda, trying to spread their philosophy and their doctrine. This is the icon for the American Humanist Association: “Good without God.” Don’t need no God. The humanist manifesto, as we shared earlier, the humanist manifesto created in [unclear] and 30s says there is no God, the, the universe always existed, it was not created, prayer will not help anyone, the Bible is just a book of myths with a lot of errors in it, a lot of, uh, erroneous things in it, contradictory things. They said all this in the manifesto. In the manifesto they said that the institutes and the associations, the families and the churches have to be converted, they have to be rebuilt, and they got to be rebuilt and converted to what we say that will help humanity and mankind. That’s right in their manifesto, okay. They also said that the present financial system of America, which was capitalism, is obsolete, and we
What does he mean by “past tense,” and what is secular humanism?

Psalm 9:19-20: Arise, O LORD, Do not let man prevail; Let the nations be judged in Your sight. Put them in fear, O LORD, That the nations may know themselves to be but men. Selah Isaiah 34:1-2: Come near, you nations, to hear; And heed, you people! Let the earth hear, and all that is in it, The world and all things that come forth from it. For the indignation of the LORD is against all nations, And His fury against all their armies; He has utterly destroyed them, He has given them over to the slaughter.
What does he say the propaganda war in the schools is, and what does he say about charity?

He says “we are in a propaganda war, we are in a war of philosophy,” and says humanists declared they would win in the public schools and universities. He says that charitable giving is used to argue that “you don’t need God to be good,” and that churches that focus on social programs have fallen into that, while “the gospel of Jesus Christ for salvation is the highest level.” He names wealthy donors in the transcript; those names are not repeated here.
What does he say the propaganda war in the schools is, and what does he say about charity?

must give everybody their fair share. We need social programs, social programs is the answer to America and mankind’s problems, right in their manifesto. And most Christians do not understand that we are in a propaganda war, we are in a war of philosophy, a war of speech, not always with guns and tanks and airplanes, but speech. And they said publicly, and they declared it emphatically, that the war they were going to wage was going to be in the public school classrooms and the universities of America, and they said, “We will win this war because we have them five days a week and the church only has a fraction of them for one hour on Sunday.” And, folks, 80 years have gone by, they pretty much won this battle. They got Christians dumbed down that we can’t even think right anymore, and this is people that publicly declare there is no God, the Gentiles, the ungodly, no Jesus, no Bible, they publicly declare it. Here is a advertisement for the, uh, humanistic religion, put out by the Secular Student Alliance. Secular Student Alliance, Billy Gates, we all know him, the second richest person in the world, they said donated 26 billion to charity. Billy Gates is good without God, they said. The third richest person, Warren Buffett, pledged to give 90%, of, 99% of his wealth to charity when he dies. Warren Buffett is good, they said, without God. What’s their emphasis? If you have a social program, you are good. You don’t need God to be good, and what’s their good? Helping somebody. Helping somebody. And the church has fallen into that. Many of the churches in America are centered now on social programs, and they think because they help people that they have attained the highest level of Christianity, and it’s not true. The gospel of Jesus Christ for salvation is the highest level, and to grow in him, that is the goal of God.
What does Isaiah 34:4 say about the heavens being rolled up?

He says it is unfair that humanists can teach in classrooms while believers cannot. He reads Isaiah 34:4, that “all the host of heaven shall be dissolved,” and says that is the “when” of God’s dealing with the nations. He says it “takes a supernatural God to perform something like this” and that people who call it an allegory will find out.
What does Isaiah 34:4 say about the heavens being rolled up?

Amen, amen. You can’t substitute that, but they’ve got us dumbed down. The religion of secular humanism, clergy in the classroom, this book. You see, they said, say there has to be a separation of church and state, but it’s okay for humanists to go into the classrooms and teach their religion in the classrooms, but no one that believes the Bible, no one that believes in Christ has a right to go in, it’s, it’s, it’s bigoted, it’s not fair, it’s not the American way. Could that be an amen? Hallelujah. And we let them get away with it. So we’re going to go on in Isaiah 34, and we’re going to see clarity of God dealing with the Gentiles. This is very powerful. When will he deal with them? Isaiah 34:4, “All the host of heaven shall be dissolved,” they will decay. Now, folks, that’s a big undertaking. The universe is huge, and God says there’s going to be a time when it’s going to decay, it’s going to rot away, it’s going to be dissolved. That’s the when, okay. “The heavens shall be rolled up like a scroll.” Now, that’s a big undertaking, this universe is huge, and God say he going to roll it up as a scroll. You roll a scroll up, you still have part of the scroll there. “All their host,” all the stars, all the planets, “shall fall down as a leaf from the vine,” and the [unclear].
What does Isaiah 34:4 say about the heavens being rolled up?

Isaiah 34:4-6: All the host of heaven shall be dissolved, And the heavens shall be rolled up like a scroll; All their host shall fall down As the leaf falls from the vine, And as fruit falling from a fig tree. “For My sword shall be bathed in heaven; Indeed it shall come down on Edom, And on the people of My curse, for judgment. The sword of the LORD is filled with blood, It is made overflowing with fatness, With the blood of lambs and goats, With the fat of the kidneys of rams. For the LORD has a sacrifice in Bozrah, And a great slaughter in the land of Edom.
Why does he say Edom and Esau picture the Gentile humanist?

He says God speaks of “Edom, the people of my curse,” and links it to Hebrews 12, where Esau “for one morsel of meat sold his birthright.” He calls that “your social program,” and says the birthright to us today is “being born again, born of the word, born of the Spirit.”
Why does he say Edom and Esau picture the Gentile humanist?

Folks, a sun, our sun is 100 times bigger than our earth, and there’s all kinds of suns out there. A sun, a star is one that radiates light, planets and other things reflect light. Okay, now, it takes a supernatural God to perform something like this. People say, “Well, it’s just an allegory,” like, uh, uh, Fox News guy Bill [unclear], “Yeah, it’s just a book, it’s an allegory.” We’ll see, we’ll see if it’s an allegory. All right, you know, they got us so dumbed down, we just think like they tell us to think. Now, “my sword shall be bathed in heaven, indeed it shall come down on Edom.” So now he’s talking about the who, he’s talking about the when, “I show wonders in the heavens,” and who is going to be influenced at that time? “I’m going to come down on Edom, the people of my curse.” A curse is something that is put on someone that they can’t change, something bad’s going to happen to them. And he used the word Edom, why? Because in Hebrews 12:6, “lest there be any fornicator or godless person,” Gentile, humanist, “as Esau.” Esau is Edom, who for one morsel of meat sold his birthright.
